name: Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) Injury
summary: Partial or complete PCL injury causing posterior tibial laxity, commonly after a dashboard injury or fall onto a flexed knee.

looksLike: Difficulty decelerating, descending stairs or running
firstSteps: Avoid posterior tibial sag and hamstring loading early when prescribed

tests.name: Posterior Drawer Test
tests.purpose: Assess posterior tibial translation relative to femur.
tests.positive: Increased posterior translation or soft endpoint compared with other side.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Avoid posterior tibial sag and hamstring loading early when prescribed
Use PCL-specific brace/orthopaedic plan where indicated
dose: Straight-leg raise if no lag: 3 x 8–12
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Introduce closed-chain strengthening within safe ranges
Gradually restore balance and functional control
dose: Leg press/shallow squat within protocol: 3 x 8–12
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Progress running, deceleration and sport-specific drills
Add hamstring loading according to healing stage and specialist protocol
Return only after objective strength and stability review
dose: Running and agility only after clearance; 2–4 sets of graded drills
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Stable posterior laxity for intended activity
Quadriceps strength and hop/landing capacity restored

structures: Possible posterolateral corner, meniscus or cartilage injury
mechanism: Direct blow to proximal tibia with knee flexed
classification: Grade I–III based on posterior translation; associated injuries alter management
investigations: Radiographs for trauma/fracture; MRI to define PCL and associated injuries when indicated.
Urgent orthopaedic assessment for high-grade or multiligament injury.
manual: Gentle ROM and patellofemoral mobility may help stiffness.
Avoid posterior tibial mobilisation or hamstring loading that increases posterior sag early.
modalities: Brace and crutches according to injury grade and orthopaedic protocol.
NMES may assist quadriceps activation; passive modalities are adjunctive.
mistakes: Treating PCL like ACL without posterior-sag precautions
pearls: Quadriceps strengthening is prioritised early in many PCL protocols.
Injury grade and associated structures determine protection and progression.

tests.name: Posterior Drawer Test
tests.purpose: Assess posterior tibial translation relative to femur.
tests.positive: Increased posterior translation or soft endpoint compared with other side.
tests.patientPosition: Supine, hip flexed 45° and knee 90°; foot stabilised, clinician applies posterior force to proximal tibia.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Supports PCL injury; assess posterior sag and associated ligament/neurovascular injury.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
